title: Praying alone
hook: without ten people some parts are skipped, but the prayer still counts

segments.voice: Yesterday, the omer, counted up at nightfall. Your line was count by night. What number did you say out loud? Today, what happens when you're the only one in the room. Day six hundred thirteen.

A hospital waiting room at six in the morning. A soldier on a base far from any synagogue. A student in a dorm who just isn't going to make it to services. A grandmother at her kitchen window before anyone else is up. We've spent weeks on this path walking through the service as a congregation says it: the leader, the answers, the ten. But on any given morning, some Jews pray with a congregation, and some pray by themselves. What happens to the prayer then?
screen: `A HOSPITAL WAITING ROOM.` → `A KITCHEN WINDOW.` → `ONE PERSON, ALONE.`

segments.voice: First, what's missing. Jewish law says certain parts are matters of holiness, said only with a minyan of ten. Without ten, you leave out Barchu, the call to prayer. You leave out the Kedushah, the holy, holy, holy said standing together. The leader's repetition of the Amidah. The Torah reading. And the Kaddish, which we met earlier on this path. Those are real losses, and the rabbis didn't pretend otherwise. The Talmud says that a prayer said with the community is especially welcome, and it encourages someone alone to pray at the same time the congregation does, so they're joined in time if not in place. But here's the other half. The heart of the service, the Shema and the Amidah, is complete when you say it alone. It counts. Fully. And the model for the silent Amidah is one woman praying by herself. Hannah, in the book of Samuel, at the sanctuary in Shiloh, with no one praying alongside her. In the old Jewish translation: "Now Hannah, she spoke in her heart; only her lips moved, but her voice could not be heard." The priest who saw her thought she was drunk. The Talmud draws lessons for all prayer from that one scene: pray with intention, move your lips, keep your voice quiet. So the silent Amidah, said by a whole congregation standing together, is built on a woman praying alone. The congregation, at its quietest moment, is copying her.
screen: `WITHOUT TEN: NO BARCHU, NO KEDUSHAH.` · `PRAY WHEN THE CONGREGATION PRAYS.` · `THE HEART OF IT IS COMPLETE.` · `HANNAH, ALONE AT SHILOH.` · then, large: `ALONE STILL COUNTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray alone once. Or, if prayer isn't yours, sit alone with intention. Settle, and breathe. Notice there's no one to follow, no one to answer you. Do what Hannah did. Let your lips move, and keep your voice too low to hear. Say something real: a thanks, a worry, a hope. If you'd like, picture all the other people, in kitchens and waiting rooms, doing the same thing right now. The bell holds the time.
Praying alone. Without ten, some parts drop away, but the Shema and the Amidah are whole, and the silent prayer is modeled on Hannah.
Your line: alone still counts. Today, do one quiet thing you'd usually only do with others, and let it count. Day six hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: Someone praying without a minyan says the Shema, its blessings and the Amidah in full, and leaves out Barchu, Kedushah, the repetition of the Amidah, the Torah reading and the Kaddish; many try to pray at the same time as their community's service.

myth: a prayer said alone doesn't count in Jewish law
the Shema and the Amidah are complete when said alone.
it's one of the matters of holiness said only with ten.
the silent Amidah is modeled on Hannah's prayer
only her lips moved; her voice could not be heard.

fork.setup: you're a priest at Shiloh. a woman is praying silently, lips moving, no sound. what did Eli think?
fork.reveal: Eli thought she was drunk. the Talmud makes her quiet, intent prayer the model for the Amidah.

original.note: Hebrew: an individual, the word Jewish law uses for someone praying without a minyan.

trapdoor: what you thought: real prayer needs a congregation.
what it means: without ten some parts drop away, but the heart of the prayer is whole.
what a scholar hears: Berakhot 8a on praying in the 'acceptable time' with the community; Berakhot 31a draws the Amidah's rules from Hannah.
